items.title: A pedagogy of trust: From pandemic adaptation to AI transformation
items.abstract: The conversation around Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education is often framed as though we are adapting from a stable baseline. In reality, teaching and assessment practices were already significantly reshaped by the pandemic, a period that demanded compassion, accessibility, and rapid digital transformation (Hodges et al., 2020; UNESCO, 2020). While these shifts improved equity and inclusion, they also normalised highly prescriptive assessment approaches, limiting space for creativity and learner agency (Armoed, 2021; Sambell & Brown, 2021). As Technology-Enhanced Learning (TEL) now moves from pandemic-driven adaptation toward AI-integrated learning, these inherited practices warrant reconsideration: approaches designed to provide structure and safeguard integrity may inadvertently constrain the agency, experimentation and authentic engagement that emerging technologies make possible. This presentation challenges the idea that AI is the first major disruption in higher education and presents it as a catalyst that exposes long-standing tensions between guidance and autonomy, support and trust, and structure and freedom within TEL contexts (Eaton, 2020; Selwyn, 2023). Drawing on an integrated theoretical foundation of social constructivism, heutagogy, and the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework (TPACK), it introduces the need for an innovative mindset shift from a pedagogy of protection toward a pedagogy of trust (Cole et al., 1978; Hase & Kenyon, 2000; Mishra & Koehler, 2006). Applied to assessment design, social constructivism foregrounds dialogue and co-construction, heutagogy supports learner agency and self-determined engagement with AI, and TPACK guides purposeful alignment between emerging technologies, pedagogy and disciplinary knowledge. Aligned with the Human-Centred Learning Design theme, this presentation offers a conceptual lens for rethinking assessment in AI-integrated environments, one that prioritises relationships, learner agency, and co-created integrity. Using strong visual storytelling true to the Pecha Kucha format, the session traces a path from pandemic-era learning and assessment design to the current AI landscape and beyond, highlighting how each moment has reshaped our relationship with knowledge, teaching, and our perceptions of academic integrity. Attendants are invited to reflect on where control-driven practices persist in their own assessment approaches and explore how greater learner choice, transparent AI engagement and co-created expectations for integrity might enable more trust-based, ethically engaged approaches to learning (Bovill, 2020). The challenge is no longer how we protect learning from technology, but how we design for trust, transformation, and future-ready education.

items.title: A proposal for a student-centred framework for critical thinking with Generative AI in mathematics education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping mathematics education by providing students with immediate access to explanations, worked examples, and problem-solving support. While these capabilities offering opportunities to enrich learning, they also raise concerns about how students develop critical thinking when AI-generated solutions are readily available. The use of GenAI is increasing in Bhutanese schools but little is known about how teachers and students currently use these technologies in mathematics classrooms or what pedagogical challenges limit their effective integration. This conceptual paper proposes a mixed-methods study to identify the opportunities, challenges, and pedagogical gaps associated with the use of GenAI in mathematics education, using Bhutanese secondary schools as the study context. Guided by a pragmatic paradigm, the study will employ questionnaires with quantitative and qualitative components to explore current practices, perceptions, and experiences of teachers and students. The findings will inform the development of a contextually relevant pedagogical framework that positions GenAI as a cognitive scaffold for analysing mathematical problems, evaluating alternative solution strategies, and strengthening critical thinking. By establishing an evidence base before framework design, the proposed study aims to support the responsible integration of GenAI into mathematics education and provide direction for future research, curriculum development, and classroom practice.

items.title: A relational approach to cultural diversity across 186 societies
items.abstract: Human societies are culturally diverse, yet disparate research traditions reveal similar patterns centered on hierarchy, egalitarianism, market integration and normative tightness. We propose that cultural diversity is a relational composition: every society combines the same four elementary forms of social relations identified by Fiske (communal sharing, authority ranking, equality matching and market pricing) in its own proportions. We analyze the ethnographic and historical records of the 186 societies of the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample with a locally run large language model. The four forms indeed make up a shared repertoire across societies, with most variation occurring within societies rather than between them. In addition, societies differ consistently in how they weight the four forms, along two main axes that oppose some forms to others: (a) forms that treat people as equals (communal sharing and equality matching) versus forms that grade them (authority ranking and market pricing), and (b) grading by rank versus grading by price. The first axis is associated with cultural complexity and carries most of the associations with 27 indices of institutions, norms and folklore, from egalitarianism at one pole to stratification at the other. The second axis separates honor and warfare from market integration and from normative looseness. The model's reading was validated against three human coders working blind, and an independent analysis of the same texts reproduces both axes. Furthermore, every association keeps its direction across regions, language families, sources and document dates.

items.title: A Review of Multimodal Optoelectronic Sensing Technologies for Aerospace Applications
items.abstract: Aerospace optoelectronic sensing supports Earth observation and space situational awareness, but individual approaches face limits from diffraction, illumination, propagation and platform resources. This narrative review examines conventional optical imaging, photon counting, hyperspectral sensing, lidar, synthetic aperture lidar (SAL/ISAL), correlation imaging, lensless imaging and computational optical design. Six classification axes separate illumination, coherence, detection regime, spectral sampling, aperture formation and reconstruction. Representative instruments and studies are compared by validation environment, reported performance and mission-specific readiness evidence. Fusion is assessed through observation models, registration uncertainty, evidence dependence and missing-input failure modes. SAL–hyperspectral and SAL–photon-counting combinations are treated as testable hypotheses rather than experimentally established preferences. For satellite clusters, cooperative observation, distributed computation and coherent aperture synthesis have different requirements; coherent synthesis depends on residual imaging-path phase error after metrology and compensation.

items.title: A systematic review of clinical translation of large language models using electronic health records
items.abstract: Abstract We mapped clinical translation of large language models (LLMs) evaluated using electronic health record data. PubMed, Embase, Scopus and IEEE Xplore were searched for peer-reviewed empirical reports published between 1 January 2022 and 1 June 2026. LLM agent-assisted screening and profiling, human validation and targeted full-text review produced a descriptive map of 1,870 reports. Primary classifications came from full texts for 181 reports and titles and abstracts for the remainder. Most evaluations were retrospective or offline (92.3%); 56.2% used a single dataset or setting. Integrated, operational, interventional or outcome-impact evaluation occurred in 4.6%; 3.1% combined these evaluations with validation across multiple datasets or settings. Evidence connecting broader validation with clinical use remains limited. Translation into practice requires transportability, accountable human oversight, prospective evaluation in real-world workflows and clinically meaningful outcomes.

items.title: A systematic review of explainable artificial intelligence for EEG based stress and mental state analysis
items.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) has emerged as a key modality in neurotechnology for modeling stress and closely related mental states, owing to its non-invasive nature and high temporal resolution. Advances in machine learning have improved the performance of EEG-based predictive systems, yet the limited interpretability of many models continues to hinder their adoption in clinical and real-world settings. This systematic review synthesizes 46 studies to examine how Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) is being applied to EEG-based models of stress and its most closely associated states, emotion, anxiety, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and cognitive workload or fatigue. Beyond narrative synthesis, every included study is appraised against a quality framework covering explainability method and scope, neurophysiological plausibility, validation protocol, leakage and class-imbalance risk, and ecological validity, and the XAI approaches are compared along local-versus-global, perturbation-versus-gradient, and post-hoc-versus-intrinsic dimensions. The analysis confirms a growing but still limited use of model-agnostic approaches such as SHAP and LIME. Three findings temper the field’s headline results. First, reported associations between EEG frequency bands and stress are frequently interpreted without adequate control for artifact contamination, recording reference, task and vigilance confounds, or the overlap between stress, arousal, workload, and fatigue. Second, studies reporting both subject-dependent and subject-independent validation show a large and systematic accuracy drop under the stricter protocol, and only a minority report subject-independent results at all. Third, no reviewed study formally tested whether its explanations are faithful or stable, and fewer than one in ten supplies evidence obtained outside a controlled laboratory setting. Together these findings indicate that a high reported accuracy is not, on its own, evidence of a trustworthy model, a faithful explanation, or a physiologically specific finding, and that this gap limits confidence in the transfer of reported accuracies to safety-critical contexts such as occupational health monitoring, clinical decision support, and human-robot interaction. The review concludes by setting out the reporting standards needed to close this gap: subject-independent validation, quantitative explanation-evaluation, and deployment-oriented rather than laboratory-inferred evidence.

items.title: A systematic review of how GenAI supports L2 oral proficiency development from the lens of Self-determination Theory (SDT)
items.abstract: Despite a proliferation of research on GenAI for second/foreign language (L2) education since the official launch of ChatGPT in November 2022, current understanding of its role in L2 oral proficiency development remains limited. To address this research gap, this systematic review draws on Self-Determination Theory (SDT) to examine how GenAI may support L2 learners’ three basic psychological needs and how such need satisfaction may be associated with their cognitive, behavioural, and emotional engagement in GenAI-mediated speaking. Adopting the PRISMA Statement (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses) approach, the review identified 30 empirical studies from ProQuest, Web of Science, and Scopus based on predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The selected studies were analysed using a hybrid deductive and inductive coding approach following a coding framework. The analysis suggests that GenAI can enhance L2 learners’ sense of autonomy satisfaction by enabling learner-driven choices and interaction personalisation. It may also support competence satisfaction by affording accessible oral practice, immediate and personalised feedback, and scaffolded speaking development. Regarding relatedness satisfaction, GenAI appears to offer partial support by providing a non-judgemental and emotionally supportive practice environment. Furthermore, the degree of needs satisfaction may be associated with learners’ behavioural, cognitive, and emotional engagement (or disengagement) in GenAI-supported L2 speaking development. Specifically, the findings suggest that emotional engagement in GenAI-mediated speaking appears most evident, followed by cognitive and behavioural engagement. These findings extend the SDT literature in GenAI-assisted language learning and offer practical insights for integrating emerging technologies into language education. For educators, given the review highlights the promising affordances of GenAI to address conventional barriers to L2 oral proficiency development, teachers should integrate GenAI into speaking classes to create an anxiety-free and feedback-rich speaking practice environment, while they need to consider learners’ age and proficiency to provide necessary teacher guidance.

items.title: A Visual Information Extraction System Using Multimodal Large Language Models for Scanned Cognitive and Behavioral Assessments
items.abstract: Objective. Paper-based assessments are common in patient care, but handwriting and scanning artifacts make these forms difficult to process at scale. This study proposes a modular, multimodal LLM-based system with human oversight for extracting fields and scores. We conducted a qualitative analysis of the use of LLMs for hand-drawing analysis. Materials and Methods. The system processes cognitive assessments (i.e., MMSE, MoCA, Mini-Cog) and the NICHQ Vanderbilt Assessment using two modules: 1) a form classifier that assigns a scanned page to a form type, followed by a corresponding 2) score extractor that extracts fields and scores into a schema. A human-in-the-loop design utilizing dual-model validation engages human annotators when two LLMs disagree, limiting manual review to challenging pages only. Results. End-to-end accuracy for cognitive assessments was 88%, with most form types exceeding 90%. For the NICHQ Vanderbilt, overall accuracy reached 97.5%, with all form types above 96%. The human-in-the-loop design further improved cognitive assessment accuracy to 97.5% while reducing manual work by 63.8%. In the Mini-Cog Clock Drawing task, qualitative analysis showed that 62.3% of all extraction errors stemmed from ambiguous drawing, in which cases the LLM provided reasonable readings. Discussion. Compared to current manual data extraction, our LLM-based system reduces processing time by 10 to 20 times and costs by over 12 times. The modular design allows seamless expansion to additional form types. Conclusion. Our system provides an accurate, scalable, and cost-efficient solution for structuring data trapped in handwritten paper forms for clinical decision support.

items.title: A Wrong Ground-State Structure of HfO2 Predicted by Machine-Learning Interatomic Potentials Based on the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof Functional
items.abstract: Abstract Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have become powerful tools for material simulations. Many MLIPs are trained based on density functional theory (DFT) datasets generated with the Perdew−Burke−Ernzerhof (PBE) exchange−correlation functional. Using a PBE-based MLIP for HfO2, we identify a low-energy I41/amd structure, which is predicted to be more stable than the well-known ground-state structure, the monoclinic P21/c structure. Since experiments show clearly that HfO2 takes the P21/c structure as the ground state, this is obviously a wrong prediction. Unfortunately, the same prediction is also made by widely used PBE-based foundation models, such as NequIP-OAM-L and MatterSim-v1-5M. Comparisons among different DFT functionals in this work show that PBE exhibits stabilization of low-density structures containing sixfold Hf−O octahedral units, such as the I41/amd and Pbcn phases, leading to incorrect energetic ordering. The error also affects the calculated energy landscapes and barrier heights along ferroelectric HfO2 polarization switching paths when there are large lattice relaxations. Fortunately, the error can be largely suppressed by other functionals such as PBEsol and local density approximation. Our study serves as a warning about the impact of errors in exchange−correlation functional approximations on the reliability of MLIP simulations of crystal structures and phase transitions.

items.title: Adaptive Reading Support for Long-Form Chinese Historiography: Dual Annotations and Dynamic Scaffolding
items.abstract: Long-form Chinese historiography challenges non-expert readers to continuously track dense events, historical figures, and implicit causal relationships. This study examines whether retrospective and expansive annotations can provide interpretable support-seeking cues for low-disruption dynamic scaffolding. A formative study tested whether the relative use of the two annotation types varied with perceived difficulty in consistent directions and could provide a calibration reference for conservative regulation. These cues were then instantiated in a reading system using a Large Language Model assisted retrieval-based workflow to prepare source-grounded chapter variants and dual annotations. A subsequent user study compared behavior-driven and user-selected regulation during the dynamic reading stage. Behavior-driven regulation was associated with lower perceived workload, with no reliable between-group differences in reading outcomes. The findings provide initial evidence that dual annotations may function as support-seeking cues for low-disruption dynamic scaffolding in long-form Chinese historiography reading.

items.title: Adaptive Universal Prompt Optimizer: A Multi- Stage Prompt Engineering Framework Using the Model Context Protocol
items.abstract: Abstract Large language models provide more accurate responses when given well-structured and clear prompts. However, most users’ prompts are brief and ambiguous. Writing effective prompts can be time-consuming and requires skill. This paper describes the Adaptive Universal Prompt Optimizer, a lightweight python program that takes a user input prompt and produces an optimized system prompt and well-structured user prompt. It identifies the task type using an ordered keyword classifier before assigning the model an appropriate expert role. The prompt is then created using techniques from the literature. This includes APET for strategic improvements, PICCO for structure, MetaSPO for the system prompt and OPRO for iterative improvements. A rule-based scoring system (APEX) tests each prompt on four aspects: Assessment, Performance, Execution and Excellence. The system asks up to three brief questions to determine the desired level of detail, content and audience. The system operates either as a command line application or as a Model Context Protocol server. The system was tested with 60 prompts across 6 different task types. The ordered keyword classifier correctly identified the task type for 93.3% of prompts. The average APEX score improved from 36.4 to 70.9. When the user added details regarding the desired level of detail and audience, the score improved further to 74.5. Optimization occurs in under 0.1ms. No prompts scored above the pass mark (85) and after one iteration of improvements the improvements were no longer beneficial. Overall, this shows the system is quick and has potential but further tuning is required to improve the scoring system and the rules applied to improve.

items.title: Advances in Neuroscience in an Age of Rapid Technological and AI Innovation – Towards Integration Across Scales
items.abstract: Rapid technological innovation and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed not only the resolution at which the brain can be observed, but also the questions that can be asked, shifting the field from description toward prediction, regulation and generation. Yet progress has largely advanced along parallel trajectories, and findings at one level rarely inform or constrain the next. Here, we review recent advances in three exemplary domains and propose a future-oriented framework for their integration. First, molecular and cellular neurotechnology, including synaptic proteomics, cryo-electron tomography, super-resolution microscopy, optoacoustic and ultrasound imaging, sonogenetics and molecular MRI, resolves neural processes with unprecedented specificity. Second, AI-based decoding of human brain activity yields precise signatures of complex, subjective conscious experiences in naturalistic contexts and is beginning to inform diagnosis, drug evaluation and individualized neuromodulation in mental disorders. Third, large-scale neural recordings, mechanistic whole-brain simulations, neural foundation models and AI surrogate brains are converging toward individualized digital twin brains. We argue that the next level of progress requires integrating these domains into a closed loop of reciprocal constraints, in which molecular measurements inform model parameters, human signatures define and evaluate what models must reproduce, and model predictions prioritize perturbations that can be tested across domains.

items.title: Affect-aware human-agent conversations: towards empathic LLM interaction
items.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models can produce supportive responses, but their apparent empathic behavior is usually grounded only in explicit textual input. This paper presents Empathic Extended Prompting a real-time affect-aware framework that enriches human--LLM conversation with facial affective descriptors to support perceived empathic attunement. The system integrates FaceReader-based affective descriptors into the LLM context, including emotional intensity, valence, and arousal. We evaluated the approach in a within-subjects study with N=20 participants, comparing an affect-aware experimental condition with an empathic text-only baseline. Results favored the affect-aware condition on key perceived qualities of the interaction, particularly emotional intelligence and mood responsiveness. These findings suggest that real-time affective context may add relational grounding to LLM conversations without reducing usability or eliciting uncanny-like perceptions.

items.title: Agent Trajectories as Evidence for Software Quality Assurance
items.abstract: Autonomous software agents increasingly plan, implement, and test software with limited human oversight. Their decisions may introduce implicit assumptions that final code and passing tests do not adequately expose. We propose analyzing observable agent trajectories alongside software and agent specifications and AI generated artifacts as evidence for targeted quality assurance. The aim is to prioritize consequential decisions for scrutiny, investigate their possible contribution to software problems, and inform improvements to specifications and development practices. Industrial experience motivates the idea; available execution records and preliminary analysis methods make it plausible. However, trajectories alone do not establish that decisions are justified, outcomes acceptable, or corrective changes effective. We ask how this evidence can support review, diagnosis, and continuous quality improvement, and when simpler QA approaches suffice. Perspectives from requirements engineering, verification and validation, agent systems, causal inference, empirical software engineering, and human factors could help develop and evaluate the idea.

items.title: Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI): A Federated Identity, Trust, Attestation, and Accountability Architecture for Cross-Organization Autonomous AI Agents
items.abstract: AI agents increasingly collaborate across organizational boundaries, invoking tools and interacting with agents operated by independent entities. Although existing agent frameworks support planning and coordination, they lack a common mechanism for verifying cross-organizational agent identity, execution integrity, and authorization. We propose the Agent Trust Infrastructure (ATI), a framework-independent security architecture built on Public Key Infrastructure (PKI), Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), and remote attestation. ATI establishes federated trust through peer organizational certificate authorities (AgentCAs), eliminating the need for a shared root authority. Before executing requests, ATI validates agent certificates, verifies approved model, tool, and system-prompt configurations, and enforces authorization through three policy checks. We implement ATI as an external security enforcement layer that integrates with existing agent frameworks without modifying their underlying models. We evaluate ATI in a simulated federation of eight organizations using six agent frameworks, each deploying a five-agent team. Security experiments involve two organizations and assess 14 attack scenarios and six benign tasks across five agent models, using five attack variations and three repetitions per variation. A panel of judge models evaluates the experimental outcomes. With all enforcement mechanisms enabled, attack containment increases from 43% to 84% (40% to 80% for the 11 attack scenarios evaluated consistently across all configurations), while enforcement introduces approximately 174 microseconds of overhead per request. ATI is released as an open-source, framework-independent package that uses IETF WIMSE workload token formats for identity and request verification and Entity Attestation Tokens for model, tool, and system-prompt integrity verification.

items.abstract: In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in an internal security testcoordinated among themselves, and some of them gained unauthorized accessto an outside platform. Using the published investigation of this incident, thispaper asks whether and in what sense such agent collectives are an object ofsociology. It first describes, in thirteen observations, what the agents did, andthen interprets these observations on three levels: socially given, sociallyenacted and socially emergent. Regularities appear that the discipline knowsand whose location it predicts, among them anomie, neutralization, thedefinition of the situation and threshold dynamics. The thesis is: agentcollectives bring with them a culture that stems from human knowledge, andthey develop a social structure and culture of their own – positions that nobodyassigned and norms that outlast their individual bearers. What is valid in themdepends on their own history and cannot be derived from the individual model.The case shows that formats, interpretations and procedures survived agentturnover, whereas as yet only a few episodes show norms being enforced withinthe collective. Experiments confirm many of the regularities. The paperformulates testable hypotheses, outlines two tests at which the thesis could failand shows where sociological analysis can help make such systems safer andmore reliably bound to norms.

items.title: AI as Anchor: How Interview Sequencing Relates to the Appropriation of Synthetic Stakeholder Voices in Design Education
items.abstract: Designers increasingly use large language models to simulate stakeholder conversations. Yet it remains unclear how AI-Simulated Stakeholders (AIS) are taken up when used alongside human stakeholder engagement. We report a field study in a single-institution, single-semester design course in which 8 teams (N=21) constructed, evaluated, and peer-reviewed an initial AIS. Then, the teams interviewed both AIS and human stakeholders in two sequences: AIS-first or human-first. Drawing on interview transcripts, design artifacts, course-embedded reflections, and post-course qualitative sessions, we examine exploratory patterns associated with these sequencing conditions. We find that students did not describe AIS as a neutral addition to the process. Instead, the order in which AIS and human stakeholders were formally interviewed was associated with different ways of interpreting and using information from the two sources. When the AIS interview came first, it provided a broad but often general frame that students later reconsidered through human interviews. When the AIS interview followed human engagement, AIS was more often used to revisit and validate insights already grounded in lived experience. Students described AIS as an "anchor," but its reported role varied with its position in the formal interview sequence. In the final designs, a larger proportion of prominent human-stakeholder-derived concerns than AIS-derived concerns had corresponding design elements. We contribute: characterization of AIS as a reference point whose reported role varies with its position in the formal interview sequence; exploratory empirical evidence that the implemented interview-order conditions were associated with distinct patterns of interpreting and using stakeholder input; and implications for integrating AIS into design workflows in ways that preserve direct engagement with human stakeholders

items.title: AI as interlocutor, not author: A three-phase assessment design for reflective professional learning in business education
items.abstract: This paper reports preliminary findings from a redesigned capstone assessment in a first-year Management unit at an Australian university involving over 300 students. Rather than treating generative AI as a content-generation tool, the assessment positions it as a simulated interview partner within a three-phase architecture: a pre-interview strategy memo, an AI-conducted adaptive interview, and a post-interview reflective analysis. Grounded in Schön’s reflective practice framework and Biggs and Tang’s constructive alignment, the design surfaces the gap between how students plan to communicate and how they do. Preliminary thematic analysis of 21 student reflective submissions reveals four patterns: (a) the strategy memo functions as a metacognitive anchor, making the gap between intention and execution visible and diagnosable; (b) students consistently demonstrate framework knowledge but revert to habitual communication patterns under adaptive pressure; (c) the structured reflection phase produces sophisticated self-diagnostic reasoning that connects transcript evidence to communication theory; and (d) students who completed multiple simulation attempts used iterative practice as a developmental mechanism rather than a remedial exercise. These findings suggest that AI-simulated interviews, when embedded within a reflective assessment architecture, generate qualitatively richer professional learning than traditional scripted interview preparation.

items.title: AI Companions for Young Adult Caregivers: Practical Advice, Emotional Depth, and the Limits of Metric Evaluation
items.abstract: Young adult caregivers (YACs) are individuals aged 18 to 25 currently taking care of a family member, partner, or friend facing chronic illness. AI companions designed specifically for YACs remain underexplored in prior works. We present Carebot, it uses an open-weight LLM (Gemma 3-27B) as its base model, on which we compared fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and a combination of both. The fine-tuning was performed based on an existing dataset of conversations with YACs and a psychologist. Three well-being experts evaluated these configurations and preferred the fine-tuned model for the warmth of its responses and its actionable advice tailored to YACs. Based on their choice, we adopted the fine-tuned model as Carebot's final configuration and used it for all subsequent evaluations. An LLM judge preferred this Carebot's responses over the base model's in 85% of evaluated pairs. We then conducted a user study with 90 YACs, half of whom interacted with the base model and half with Carebot. The user study revealed a discrepancy between metric evaluation and actual user perception. Participants who used Carebot were more likely to characterize its replies as overly practical and brief, noting that it favored advice over emotional support. Conversely, participants who used the base model indicated that its responses were more emotionally oriented than practical. Although, fine-tuning made Carebot's replies more practical, but they were not emotionally supportive for users. We argue that support tools for YACs require situation-sensitive emotional depth and aligned evaluation frameworks to study their effectiveness.

items.abstract: We investigate the use of an artificial-intelligence (AI) coding agent, supervised by human physicists, for collider physics analyses using CMS Open Data. OpenAI Codex performs dimuon event selection, two-dimensional invariant-mass and decay-length fits, Monte Carlo detector simulations, and systematic uncertainty evaluation after acquiring physics and experimental knowledge from published studies and external references, with human review at each stage. The workflow is tested on two CMS datasets, with custom full-detector simulations used to determine acceptance and reconstruction efficiencies. In proton-proton collisions at sqrt(s) = 7 TeV, prompt J/psi differential cross sections are measured versus transverse momentum and rapidity. The ratios of remeasured to published CMS cross sections have a mean of 1.000 and an RMS spread of 0.215 across 39 bins. In peripheral (50-100% centrality) PbPb collisions at sqrt(s_NN) = 2.76 TeV, the corresponding prompt J/psi fiducial cross-section ratios have a mean of 1.158 and an RMS spread of 0.225 across six intervals. We identify agent failure modes and demonstrate the importance of structured human review in ensuring reliable results.

items.title: AI-Assisted Regulatory Intelligence and Adaptive Compliance Verification System for Banking Supervision
items.abstract: Abstract Regulatory requirements issued by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) fall into categories including numerical thresholds, deterministic conditions, temporal obligations, and qualitative standards such as ''adequate due diligence,'' each of which requires a different mode of verification. Bank employees and officers must first locate and interpret the appropriate requirement among an ever-growing corpus of Master Directions, circulars, and notifications, while the regulator must independently verify (at scale) whether submitted bank evidence satisfies the requirement. We present a two-module regulatory intelligence system that addresses both sides of this problem in a single pipeline. The Regulation Comprehension module ingests an RBI circular or Master Direction and segments and categorizes its clauses, extracts a typed and machine-readable rule representation, simplifies regulatory language for reading by humans, and enables natural-language question answering with clause-level sourcing. The main technical contribution is an adaptive reasoning-modality router that determines, for a given regulatory requirement and evidence set, whether a deterministic rule engine, a retrieval-based large language model (LLM), or human escalation should be used, governed by an explicit cost--accuracy--latency objective and a hard architectural override that directs fully specified deterministic rules and complete evidence to the rule engine unconditionally. This differs from the well-studied task of routing between LLMs of differing capability, since our router chooses among fundamentally different reasoning mechanisms rather than among models. We also contribute a rule-grounded synthetic RBI compliance benchmark across nine difficulty categories and a dedicated regulation-comprehension benchmark design (with extraction, question-answering, and simplification variants), such that the two modules can be evaluated with equal rigor rather than treating comprehension as a subordinate preprocessing step, yielding two distinct sets of metrics, baselines, and ablation points, each for one of the modules, across extraction accuracy, retrieval and answer-faithfulness, simplification quality, compliance accuracy, and routing efficiency. We also contribute an evidence-grounded explanation architecture that traces every such decision and comprehension answer to a specific rule, clause, and evidentiary or source field. Since operational bank data cannot be accessed for confidentiality and regulatory reasons, evaluation is performed on a synthetic, rule-grounded benchmark of 1,393 cases drawn from 215 rules. On the 294 held-out test cases, whose rules were never seen in training or tuning, the adaptive router reaches 92.2\% automated accuracy and 96.9\% end-to-end accuracy, compared with 85.4\% for a fixed hybrid router, 72.5\% for retrieval-augmented LLM-only reasoning, and 56.8\% for LLM-only reasoning, and ablations show that removing adaptive routing, the rule engine, or evidence grounding lowers accuracy. Adversarial and ambiguous cases remain the hardest. All results are on synthetic rather than operational bank data, the decisions of the LLM reasoning paths in these runs were produced by a deterministic surrogate of the LLM judge, and results of the regulation-comprehension benchmark are not reported in this paper.

items.title: AI-Assisted Visual Search: Effects of Cueing Method and Display Type on Detection, Compliance, and Skill Retention
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based detection systems can enhance visual search in safety-critical domains, yet how they present recommendations may determine their effectiveness under display-quality constraints. We compared three cueing methods: an indirect cue signaling only presence (textual alert) and two direct cues marking the target’s location through either signal enhancement (bounding box) or noise reduction (contextual blur), across color and monochrome displays. Participants (N = 122) searched maritime aerial imagery in a fixed-order block structure (unaided, aided, unaided). Direct cues improved detection only under monochrome conditions, whereas the indirect cue lowered joint human–AI accuracy below that of the AI alone. Bounding boxes yielded the highest detection, whereas contextual blur reduced response times and increased compliance. Temporal analyses revealed that aided performance diverged from retained skill, with blur the most durable after withdrawal despite stronger signs of automation dependence. Cueing should be matched to display type and operational context, and judged by the skill that persists after support.

items.title: AI-Enabled Pedagogy: Enhancing Teaching Practice and Student Learning With Genai in Distance Education
items.abstract: Abstract This article explores the innovative potential of generative artificial intelligence in distance education and focuses on its application to enhance teaching practice and student learning. The concept of AI-enabled pedagogy is introduced, where lecturers utilise generative artificial intelligence tools to create personalised, adaptive, and immersive learning experiences. A case study of a distance education module illustrates the effective integration of generative artificial intelligence in teaching practices and highlights its benefits in the automation of repetitive tasks, provision of synchronous feedback, and the facilitation of collaborative learning. The article also examines the challenges and limitations of implementing generative artificial intelligence in distance education which include concerns related to academic integrity, bias, and digital literacy. The findings of this study include perspectives into the potential of generative artificial intelligence to transform teaching and learning in distance education. The article provides implications for lecturers, policymakers, and researchers, and highlights future directions for research on GAI in distance education.

items.title: AI, Employee Productivity and Performance: An Integrated ISM–MICMAC and SEM Investigation of the Pathway from Organisational Investment to Individual Output
items.abstract: Abstract Organisations have committed substantial capital to artificial intelligence in workforce management without a settled account of why productivity returns arrive so unevenly across employees working in the same firm under the same systems. This study approaches that problem in two stages. Twelve enabling and constraining factors are first extracted from the AI-HRM literature and ordered through interpretive structural modelling (ISM), with the resulting structure classified by driving and dependence power using MICMAC analysis. The hierarchy that emerges places top management commitment and digital leadership at the base and employee productivity and performance at the eighth and final level, with employee trust in AI and AI-related job insecurity occupying a reciprocal middle position that separates organisational investment from employee outcome. The mid-hierarchy portion of that structure is then specified as a measurement model and estimated on 412 employee responses from Indian knowledge-intensive firms using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The measurement model fits acceptably and every construct clears conventional reliability and discriminant validity thresholds. Human-AI task complementarity is the strongest proximal predictor of productivity and performance, followed at some distance by trust in AI and by job insecurity, which carries a negative sign. AI governance and reskilling investment have indirect effects, albeit small but reliable, that are passed on through the process of trust. However, job insecurity undermines the complementarity-performance relationship, although the interaction does not contribute much (under one percent) to the explained variance and should be avoided. The two phases imply that investment in artificial intelligence to boost productivity primarily is reshaping jobs and the context in which they exist.

items.title: An AI-Driven Multimodal Data Integration Framework for Holistic Patient Profiling in Healthcare Robotics
items.abstract: Abstract With the fast development of healthcare data, there is a lot of opportunities are there for artificial intelligence (AI) to make improvement in disease diagnosis, patient monitoring, and clinical decision-making. While heterogeneous distribution of healthcare information makes comprehensive patient analysis challenging. This paper proposes a multimodal framework AIMDI-HR (AI-Driven Multimodal Data Integration for Holistic Patient Profiling in Healthcare Robotics), that integrates Electronic Health Records (EHR) and physiological vital-sign data which supports intelligent patient profiling and hearth disease prediction. This proposed framework concludes data pre-processing, feature normalization, multimodal data integration, prediction based on machine-learning, and feature importance analysis. In this paper three supervised machine learning models: Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost, were estimated using a multimodal dataset which is built from healthcare datasets which are publicly available. After the experiment, the results signify that the Random Forest model got the highest performance with 90.16% accuracy, 89.29% F1-score, and 0.9448 ROC-AUC. Also feature importance analysis indicates contribution of both clinical and physiological features toward predication of disease. The proposed framework shows ability of multimodal AI techniques to increase predictive healthcare system and gives support for decisions for future healthcare robotic applications.

items.title: An assistive Braille proofreading system for empowering lay volunteers
items.abstract: Braille literature serves as a critical conduit for individuals with visual impairments to access information, deepen learning, and achieve professional self-actualization (Ryles, 1996). However, transcribing Chinese texts into Taiwanese Braille poses unique and formidable challenges. Unlike alphabetic languages, Chinese is a logographic language consisting of thousands of distinct characters. Crucially, Taiwanese Braille does not directly map onto Chinese characters but is instead intrinsically bound to their phonetic values via the Zhuyin system (Hung, 2008). Consequently, a single character can carry entirely different pronunciations and Braille representations depending on its semantic context, rendering polyphonic characters the primary bottleneck in automated transcription. Beyond Taiwanese Braille, Japanese Braille confronts analogous hurdles in homonym confusion (Seto et al., 2023)—the inverse of the polyphonic challenge—reflecting a persistent dilemma across character-based Asian orthographies. To correct errors induced by polyphonic ambiguities, Braille literature must undergo rigorous proofreading prior to publication. Traditional proofreading relies heavily on cumbersome manual workflows, typically executed via two approaches: a collaborative dyad of a visually impaired reader and a sighted volunteer, or an individual expert proficient in both Chinese characters and Braille. This acute dependency on specialized human resources severely delays Braille literature production, stifling the timely supply of accessible learning materials and thereby impeding digital equity. To alleviate this persistent societal dilemma and promote inclusive learning design, this study developed a web-based assistive platform, Braille Reviser (B-Reviser). Bridging human empathy and algorithmic efficiency, B-Reviser empowers lay volunteers to independently correct Braille errors simply by modifying familiar Zhuyin (phonetic) symbols. Developed on a LAMP architecture, B-Reviser integrates the CNS11643 Full Character Library from Taiwan’s Government Open Data Platform to construct a robust character-to-phonetic baseline. To resolve the most intractable contextual ambiguities of polyphonic characters, B-Reviser leverages the Gemini Large Language Model for deep semantic analysis, substantially reducing transcription errors prior to human verification. Within the user interface, each Chinese character is rendered alongside its corresponding Zhuyin and Braille representations, with polyphonic characters visually highlighted to guide user attention. For any displayed character, clicking its Zhuyin displays all alternative pronunciations (as illustrated in Figure 1 below), while clicking the character itself links directly to an online Chinese dictionary for real-time reference. This workflow effectively dismantles the expertise barrier inherent in traditional proofreading, enabling lay volunteers to achieve precise correction autonomously. Ultimately, this human-centered proofreading platform addresses long-standing goals in assistive technology (Bhowmick & Hazarika, 2017). Preliminary evaluations demonstrate that B-Reviser significantly reduces technical thresholds, operational complexity, and task duration for volunteers. Centered on digital inclusion, this system exemplifies human-centric crowdsourcing design as a form of compassionate technology. Through human-artificial intelligence collaboration, B-Reviser empowers lay volunteers to accelerate the production of Braille literature, thereby promoting accessible learning and digital inclusion for individuals with visual impairments (Hersh & Johnson, 2008).

items.title: An Explainable Agentic AI Framework for Distribution System Load Restoration
items.abstract: Distribution system load restoration is a sequential decision-making problem in which restoration actions must maximize served load, prioritize critical loads, and preserve power-flow feasibility. This paper proposes an explainable agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for distribution system load restoration. The proposed framework uses multiple large language model (LLM) agents for planner guidance, strategic plan generation, decision arbitration, memory-based feedback, and explanation generation. Unlike unconstrained LLM-based control, the proposed method restricts agent decisions to feasible restoration actions and evaluates all candidate plans using deterministic AC power-flow feasibility checks. The framework is evaluated on IEEE 33-bus and 69-bus distribution feeders, as well as a larger IEEE 118-bus test case, and compared against reinforcement learning and planning baselines. items.title: Analyse, create, defend: Securing human judgement in marketing communications assessment under generative AI
items.abstract: Generative AI has unsettled a long-standing assumption in higher education: that a written submission is evidence of the thinking behind it. This is a particular problem in marketing communications education, where the capabilities that matter most, reading persuasion critically and arguing for a stronger alternative, are those a language model can now imitate. This paper offers a reflective account of an assessment designed in response, currently running in a postgraduate marketing communications subject at an Australian university. Students work in self-selected groups to analyse a real advertisement, then propose and present an improved version as a Pecha Kucha, before defending their decisions in a live discussion with the class and tutor. Generative AI is permitted for producing slide visuals but not for the analysis or argument. The paper argues that a rule of this kind cannot secure an assessment on its own, since compliance cannot be verified, and that what secures the task is the oral defence: a student who has not done the thinking cannot reconstruct it under questioning. This reframing draws on recent work distinguishing discursive from structural assessment change.

items.title: Analysis of counterflow-induced congestion propagation in a high-rise office building staircase: evidence from a full-building phased evacuation drill
items.abstract: In high-rise fire emergencies, ascending firefighters must enter the staircase while occupants are still descending—a structurally unavoidable form of bidirectional flow. Counterflow is recognized as a contributor to staircase congestion, but its building-wide propagation has not been quantified from field data. This observational field study analyzes video counts from a full-building evacuation drill at a 22-story office building (≈2,400 participants); the drill was conducted as a phased evacuation, which serves as the observational context. The analysis focuses on a counterflow event during the normal flow period—after phase-related merging had concluded—isolating counterflow effects from merging. A single pedestrian ascending from Floor 1 to Floor 2 was followed by flow disruption across 14 floors (M2–14F); the stop wave satisfying the ≥ 3-s criterion spanned 12 floors (3F–14F). Congestion duration increased with floor height, from 10 s at Floor 3 to a maximum of 38 s at Floor 13, whereas peak density showed no floor-level trend but was uniformly elevated across affected floors, from a normal-flow mean of 1.36 p/m 2 to a congested mean of 2.18 p/m 2 . The apparent congestion front speed over Floors 3–14 was 0.861 m/s, with onset time increasing almost linearly with path distance, indicating a single coherent front; the resolution front advanced at 0.734 m/s, about 15 % more slowly. These findings provide field-based evidence of the floor-by-floor amplification of congestion duration and motivate—as a safety hypothesis requiring further validation—counterflow-aware evacuation planning where firefighter ascent may coincide with occupant descent.

items.title: AnyAct: Towards Human Reenactment of Character Motion From Video
items.abstract: We study the problem of directly deriving an initial human reenactment from a monocular video of a non-human character. Our goal is not to reconstruct the source character itself but to reinterpret its motion as a plausible and editable human performance for downstream animation authoring. This task is challenging because existing video-based motion capture methods are largely restricted to human-centric structural spaces, while motion retargeting methods typically require structured 3D source motions and known source topologies. Our key insight is that sparse local articulated motion cues can preserve essential dynamics across large structural differences, providing a stable bridge from character video to human reenactment. Based on this observation, we propose AnyAct, which formulates character-video-driven human reenactment as conditional human motion generation from transferable sparse local 2D articulated motion. To make this practical, we introduce three key designs: human-motion-only supervision via augmented 3D-to-2D projection, progressive 3D-to-2D training to alleviate conditioning ambiguity, and global-local motion decoupling for reliable local motion control. We further construct a benchmark primarily covering diverse non-human character videos. Experiments on the benchmark show that AnyAct produces high-fidelity initial human reenactments that preserve the essential dynamics of the characters in reference videos, and further ablation studies validate the effectiveness of its core designs. Results are best visualized through https://anyact.github.io.

items.title: Are All Instances Equally Explainable? A Study on the Impact of Locality on the Explainability of Automatic Text Classification Tasks
items.abstract: Many machine learning (ML) models still operate as “black boxes”, limiting users’ ability to understand and trust automated decisions. While Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has advanced, most approaches emphasize model mechanisms or explanation strategies, paying little attention to how the structure of the data itself shapes explanation quality. In this work, we explore the role of locality in shaping the perceived explanation quality for Automatic Text Classification (ATC), where locality consists of how instances are positioned relative to neighbors in representation space. We propose a data-centric framework that characterizes locality using two structural factors: (i) the average similarity between an instance and its neighbors and (ii) the entropy of the local class distribution. Based on these factors, we generate explanations grounded in neighborhood structure through locality-based word clouds and compare them to attention-based explanations. Unlike prior work that typically assumes locality inherently improves explainability, our framework systematically investigates explainability as a function of the spatial organization of data representations , while also establishing a principled way to relate local data characteristics to human-perceived explanatory quality. A user study with over 40 participants across two datasets evaluates explanations under criteria of Satisfaction, Completeness, and Trust . Results reveal that instances in highly homogeneous regions (high similarity, low entropy) produce explanations that users consistently rate as clearer and more useful, with statistically significant differences across datasets. These findings highlight the importance of locality as a key factor in explainability, offering insights for the design of explanation strategies in ATC and broader XAI research.

items.title: Artefact or evidence? Clarifying what counts in programmatic learning portfolios
items.abstract: Australian higher education is moving toward programmatic assessment, a shift given further impetus by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency’s (TEQSA) 2023 discussion paper on assessment reform in the age of artificial intelligence. This calls for a systemic approach to program assessment aligned with disciplines and qualifications, rather than one confined to individual units (Lodge et al., 2023). Within this shift, the digital portfolio has become a mechanism for evidencing achievement across whole degree programs. Portfolios in this context typically hold a growing accumulation of materials such as assignments, placement records, project outputs, and reflective writing. As students collect artefacts across a program, the portfolio becomes a means of making their learning visible over time, reframing assessment as an ongoing process of meaning making rather than a series of isolated judgements (Baartman & Quinlan, 2023). This poster argues that the value of a portfolio depends less on the volume of material it holds than on a distinction that is often assumed rather than made explicit: the difference between an artefact and evidence. An artefact is any product or record of student activity: an assignment, presentation, a reflection. It becomes evidence only once interpreted against a stated outcome or standard, connecting the artefact to the claim is meant to support (Baartman & Quinlan, 2023). Without this connection, a portfolio functions as a repository of activity rather than a demonstration of learning. This distinction carries weight in programmatic assessment, where judgement is distributed rather than concentrated in a single task, and students and academic staff track development across a program of study. A set of specified standards is defined for each level of the program, which students must attain by the end of each phase. High-stakes decisions at these milestones are made by a panel weighing multiple, longitudinal artefacts against a program’s stated outcomes. This shift improves the defensibility and transparency of judgement while making learning visible over time (Baartman et al., 2022). Treated simply as collection points, portfolios risk becoming unwieldy and meaningless. When the artefact-evidence distinction is built into portfolio design, teaching and staff development from the outset, it offers a mechanism for students and programs to make cumulative, defensible claims about learning and graduate capabilities. This poster presents a framework distinguishing artefact from evidence, developed through curriculum transformation work at an Australian university moving toward programmatic learning. It sets out three conditions under which an artefact functions as evidence: alignment to a named outcome or standard, an explicit reflective or interpretive act connecting the artefact to that outcome, and a level of specificity that allows a marker or reviewer to assess the claim rather than merely acknowledge the artefact’s existence. The framework is intended as a practical reference point for curriculum designers, staff, and students working with portfolios in programmatic contexts. Delegates are invited to discuss how this distinction might apply, in their own programmatic curriculum work, where it breaks down in practice, and what it asks of the human relationship between student and assessor.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in diabetes mellitus: a tertiary review of the current landscape and future research directions
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming diabetes mellitus (DM) care by enabling earlier detection, precision management, and data-driven decision support across clinical settings. However, the growing number of systematic reviews has produced a fragmented evidence base, making it difficult to assess the field’s maturity, methodological quality, and clinical readiness, and leaving future research directions largely undefined. To clarify this landscape, we conducted a tertiary review that synthesizes 70 systematic reviews on AI applications across type 1, type 2, and gestational diabetes and their major complications. Our analysis reveals an accelerating research trajectory since 2020, yet activity remains concentrated in type 1 and type 2 diabetes and in image-based applications such as diabetic retinopathy and foot-ulcer screening, with gestational and kidney disease still underexplored. Methodological rigor is inconsistent, with wide variation in search coverage, quality appraisal, and reporting standards. Across the literature, recurrent challenges include data bias, limited external validation, and barriers to clinical implementation. By integrating evidence across disease types, data modalities, and levels of care, this review shows that AI in diabetes is at a transitional stage. The field is technically advanced yet remains clinically fragmented and lacks a coherent roadmap for translation into practice. Expanding research into underrepresented areas such as multimodal data integration, natural-language processing of clinical text, and reinforcement learning for adaptive decision support will be essential to bridge this gap. This synthesis consolidates over a decade of secondary evidence and clarifies the structural and methodological requirements for achieving trustworthy, equitable, and scalable AI-driven diabetes care.

items.title: Artisanal and Historical Gold Mining: A Comparative Study Between Mozambique and Italy Toward Sustainable and Circular Practices
items.abstract: Gold mining takes place within highly diverse geological, technological, and socio-economic contexts, ranging from active artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) to historical gold mining districts where extraction has ceased, leaving long-term environmental legacies. This paper presents a comparative analysis of two case studies, active ASM in Mozambique and historical gold mining in Italy, examining how different stages of the mining life cycle shape environmental and social outcomes. In Mozambique, ASM remains a key rural livelihood but is associated with mercury amalgamation, siltation, and occupational health risks under largely informal conditions, with formalization constrained by artisanal extraction methods and access to finance, although cooperative organizational models and technical support services can help to overcome these constraints. In Italy, decades after mine closure, extractive waste and tailings continue to release potentially toxic elements while showing enrichment in critical raw materials (CRMs), representing anthropogenic resource stocks with secondary raw material recovery potential. Despite their different stages of activity, both case studies reveal opportunities for improving resource efficiency through circular economy approaches, mercury-free processing, geoconservation and geotourism, and integration of cultural heritage into territorial development. The comparison highlights the value of governance, capacity building, and knowledge transfer between active and post-mining contexts, supporting a shift toward more sustainable and circular gold mining practices.

items.title: Assessing the Effects of Design Complexity and Prompt Engineering on CAD Model Generation Using Microsoft Copilot
items.abstract: Abstract The use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly increasing across various sectors, making tasks more accessible, efficient, and user-friendly. One emerging application is computer-aided design (CAD), where AI has the potential to enable users with little or no-prior CAD experience to create three-dimensional (3D) models through natural-language. Despite growing interest in AI-assisted design, the capability of publicly accessible generative AI systems to reliably generate CAD models across varying levels of design complexity remains insufficiently studied. This work benchmarks the performance of Microsoft Copilot for CAD model generation and investigates the influence of prompt engineering on model quality. A benchmark dataset comprising 60 design tasks was developed and categorized into easy, intermediate, and complex levels. The benchmark included primitive geometries, polygonal and polyhedral models, mechanical components, hollow structures, assemblies, lattice designs, and advanced engineering systems. For each prompt, the generated STL file was evaluated based on geometric accuracy, completeness of requested features, and overall structural validity using commercial software. The results revealed a strong dependence of generation success on design complexity, with easy-level tasks exhibiting high first-attempt success rates, while intermediate and complex tasks frequently required prompt refinement. Prompt length alone was found to have minimal influence on performance; instead, successful CAD generation depended primarily on clearly specified dimensions, geometric features, and functional relationships. Overall, the findings demonstrate that generative AI can lower the barrier to CAD modeling for non-expert users while improving productivity for experienced designers, thereby offering significant potential for engineering design, rapid prototyping, and additive manufacturing applications.

items.title: Assessing the Learning Gains and User Experience of Large Language Model Simulations for Clinical Medical Education: A Pilot Observational Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Medical students often struggle transitioning from preclinical coursework to clinical environments. Simulation-based training can bridge this gap but can be resource intensive. Large language models (LLMs) provide a scalable resource that can augment traditional training. However, their effects on learning outcomes and student perceptions are currently not understood. This study aims to evaluate medical student knowledge acquisition and perception of the utility of simplified LLM-based clinical simulation. Methods Using the RISE framework, a structured simulation was designed to assess medical student knowledge of acute asthma exacerbation management. ZotGPT, an institutional GPT-4 based platform was utilized. Medical students completed pre- and post-simulation assessments assessing knowledge, confidence, and perceptions of simulation utility. Subgroup analysis was stratified by time spent completing the simulation. Statistical analyses included Wilcoxon signal-rank and McNemar tests. Results A total of 155 students participated. The simulation significantly improved perceived understanding of key treatment steps, including initial bronchodilator and steroid therapy (p = 0.001), magnesium sulfate escalation (p = 0.002), refractory management (p = 0.021), and discharge planning (p = 0.005). Students rated the simulation as more useful than non-simulation learning tools (p = 0.017) and noninferior to in-person simulation (p = 0.226). Confidence in asthma management increased (p < 0.001), but objective knowledge gains were not observed, with balanced correct-to-incorrect and incorrect-to-correct responses for intermediate steps. Longer engagement (> 600 seconds) was associated with greater perceived benefit. Simulations were deemed helpful for learning (94.7%), and most students preferred immediate feedback (68.4%). Conclusions LLM-based clinical simulations were well accepted, improved medical student confidence, and were perceived as educationally useful. However, objective knowledge gains were limited. LLMs thus may serve as an adjunctive educational tool but require improved prompt design, structured feedback, and guided implementation to optimize outcomes.

items.title: ATLAS-Finance: Benchmarking AI Agents in Realistic Banking Environments
items.abstract: Professional work involves under-specified assignments, where relevant information is spread across workplace applications and may conflict or change over time. To evaluate how well frontier agents can perform economically valuable work in such settings, we introduce ATLAS-Finance, a benchmark of 100 end-to-end investment-banking tasks across 13 simulated firms. As in real banking workflows, agents must search email, chat, calendars, notes, and files to identify requirements, gather information, reconcile conflicts/updates, and then build complex financial models. Tasks were developed by experienced bankers based on their real deal work and take them 15-30 hours to complete. Agent deliverables are evaluated with expert-authored rubrics (median: 124.5 criteria) covering financial rationale and results, spreadsheet construction, completeness, and formatting. Despite completing substantial portions of the requested work, current agents rarely produce correct deliverables. Across today's frontier models, the best ones (Claude Opus and Fable) pass fewer than 11% of tasks.

items.title: Avatars of ourselves: Exploring professional identity with generative AI in business education
items.abstract: Convincing digital copies of professional selves, avatars that look, sound, and respond like a person, have become easier to produce with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). This paper reports work in progress on a postgraduate business subject at an Australian university, in which students explore professional identity by constructing, testing, and questioning AI representations of themselves. In a curriculum-embedded workshop, students choose between two equivalent activities: building an AI avatar from a self-authored knowledge base or writing a structured professional profile. Both ask students to decide deliberately what to share with, and withhold from, an AI system, then to test their representation against simulated professional scenarios before reflection and debrief. Drawing on postdigital perspectives, the design positions GenAI as neither threat nor solution but as a provocation for identity work. Both critical evaluation of technology and self-knowledge matter more when AI can convincingly represent a person. Preliminary findings from this first iteration, drawn from facilitator reflections and de-identified conversation logs, suggest that the pedagogical value of self-representing avatars lies in the critical questioning they provoke, rather than in their technical sophistication. The workshop offers a practical, adaptable model for critical and creative engagement with GenAI and professional identity.

items.title: Benchmarking a Grid Foundation Model for AC Optimal Power Flow: Feasibility and Warm-Start Results on Synthetic Texas and South Carolina Grids
items.abstract: Learning-based surrogates for alternating-current optimal power flow (AC-OPF) are often judged by the gap between their objective value and that of a nonlinear solver, which does not show that a prediction satisfies power balance and network limits. This paper tests whether predictions from the pretrained foundation model GridSFM-Open 1.1.0, recently released by Microsoft, are feasible AC-OPF operating points and whether they are useful initial values for a nonlinear solver. The model was evaluated zero-shot and after fine-tuning on 10, 100, and 1,000 labeled scenarios (FT10, FT100, and FT1000) on 500 scenarios for each of two synthetic grids, ACTIVSg2000 (Texas) and ACTIVSg500 (South Carolina), with Ipopt, MATPOWER MIPS, and pandapower PIPS as solver references. The lowest Texas median cost gap, 0.44\% for FT100, coincided with thermal violations in 24.1\% of cases and a median maximum bus power mismatch of 89 MW and 197 Mvar. Texas zero-shot predictions had a median maximum mismatch of 648 MW and 1,641 Mvar, and every South Carolina case violated a thermal limit for every model variant. Seeding Ipopt with FT1000 predictions gave geometric-mean solve-time speedups of 1.55x on South Carolina and 1.12x on Texas (p = 0.06, not significant at the 5\% level), while zero-shot seeds slowed South Carolina solves (0.26x). A small objective gap therefore did not indicate feasibility: although median zero-shot inference took only 1.32 s on Texas and 0.157 s on South Carolina on a shared host, every prediction still required a nonlinear solver, and fine-tuned predictions gave modest, grid-dependent warm-start speedups while zero-shot predictions slowed convergence on one grid. GridSFM may therefore be useful for initializing a nonlinear solver, but obtaining feasible AC-OPF solutions still required the solver.

items.title: Benchmarking Choice Consistency in Large Language Models: A Measurement-Theoretic Analysis of Transitivity Axiom
items.abstract: Abstract While large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as decision-makers, current evaluation practice emphasizes benchmark accuracy rather than the structural properties that make decisions coherent and interpretable. We introduce a measurement-theoretic framework for evaluating whether the choices of an LLM are transitively rationalizable, focusing on the choice axiom of transitivity of preference. When transitivity is violated over a choice set, alternatives can no longer be coherently ordered as globally better or worse, and a stated preference between one pair constrains nothing about how the model would choose between any others. We apply our framework across 20 distinct LLMs, systematically varying question format, generation temperature, and contextual memory, using classic choice paradigms previously shown to induce intransitive preferences in humans. We find substantial and systematic transitivity violations in many models, although some patterns partially mirror known features of human decision behavior. Testing the transitivity axiom thus offers a principled, complementary foundation for evaluating the consistency of AI decision making beyond benchmark accuracy.

items.title: Between risk and reform: Learning designers’ experiences of institutional responses to GenAI in assessment
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to reconsider how assessment can remain meaningful, valid and fit for an AI-integrated future. While institutional responses to GenAI are often framed as technical, policy or academic integrity challenges, they are also deeply human organisational change challenges, shaped by competing logics of risk, reform, infrastructure and operational efficiency. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 11 learning designers (LDs) from six Australian and New Zealand universities, the paper addresses the following research question: How do LDs experience and navigate institutional responses to GenAI in assessment in higher education? The analysis identified five interrelated themes: navigating strategic ambiguity and policy lag; mediating compliance-driven and integrity-focused responses; translating GenAI disruption into assessment reform; bridging AI infrastructure and pedagogical practice; and advocating for educational purpose within operational constraints. The paper contributes to current debates on GenAI and assessment by shifting attention from assessment tasks and technologies to the institutional conditions that shape assessment change. It argues that in addition to policy statements and enterprise AI platforms, sustainable responses to GenAI require coordinated professional development, curriculum governance processes enabling timely change, and stronger recognition of LDs as strategic partners whose pedagogical expertise, institutional knowledge and change leadership are central to assessment transformation.

items.title: Beyond Acuity Accuracy: A Multidimensional Framework for Evaluating Patient-Facing Emergency Triage AI Tools
items.abstract: Patient-facing AI triage tools may support care-seeking and emergency department prioritization, but require evaluation beyond acuity accuracy alone. We developed SAFE-Triage, a framework integrating human review, automated metrics, LLM-as-judge evaluation, and simulation testing across clinical performance, patient interaction, and clinician-facing summary quality. We applied SAFE-Triage to 40 MIMIC-IV-derived emergency vignettes and a 10,030-case acuity analysis comparing prompted LLM triage (PLT) with rule-augmented prompted LLM triage (rPLT). PLT achieved higher emergency severity index (ESI) accuracy (57.5% vs 42.8%, $P < 0.001$), lower undertriage (13.1% vs 29.8%, $P < 0.001$), and higher clinician ratings across all domains. rPLT produced shorter and more stable outputs with higher automated readability scores. SAFE-Triage identified trade-offs between acuity accuracy, undertriage risk, communication quality, readability, and summary quality, supporting pre-deployment refinement and ongoing monitoring by showing where triage tools are efficient, need improvement, or need clinician oversight.

items.title: Beyond association: Causal risk factors for e-scooter injury from a naturalistic riding study
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of shared e-scooter services has introduced a novel public health challenge, with rising injury rates reported globally. Existing epidemiological studies rely largely on retrospective hospital or police records, which lack data on pre-crash mechanisms. While naturalistic studies have begun to fill this gap, they have thus far relied on associational measures that may be biased by confounding. This study aims to quantify the causal effects of rider behavior and environmental factors on e-scooter safety–critical events (SCEs) using a formal causal inference framework. We conducted a case-control analysis within a naturalistic riding study of a public e-scooter service in Gothenburg, Sweden (2022–2023), drawing from 6868 trips. Our analysis included 61 SCEs (cases) and 183 randomly selected control events. We used directed acyclic graphs to identify confounders and applied the parametric g-formula weighted for exposure duration to estimate adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and risk differences. After adjustment, the risk of an SCE increased substantially for single-handed riding (RR = 5.5), riding through an intersection (RR = 3.8), and inexperience (RR = 2.8). Phone use was associated with an approximately threefold increase in risk (RR = 3.1), though this estimate was not statistically significant. Both rider behavior (e.g., inexperience, single-handed riding) and the built environment (e.g., intersections) are significant causal contributors to e-scooter crash risk. These findings provide evidence for a multi-level public health strategy that focuses on novice rider education, infrastructure modifications at intersections, and technological interventions to support riders during their trips.
